props.title: Berlin: Symphony of a Great City
props.initialSlug: A day in Berlin's life told through pure visuals

sections.content: Berlin: Symphony of a Great City revolutionized the city symphony film movement, capturing one day in Weimar-era Berlin through pure visual poetry. Director Walter Ruttmann abandoned traditional narrative, instead crafting a rhythmic montage of urban life from dawn to midnight. The film's influence echoes through later city portraits like Man with a Movie Camera (1929) and Koyaanisqatsi (1982). Ruttmann's innovative cross-cutting between machines, crowds, and architecture created a mechanical ballet that embodied both the excitement and anxiety of modernization.

sections.content: The city symphony movement emerged in the 1920s as filmmakers grappled with rapid urbanization and technological change. Manhatta (1921) by Paul Strand and Charles Sheeler first established the format, but Ruttmann perfected it. His use of rhythmic editing influenced experimental filmmakers for decades, from Maya Deren to Godfrey Reggio. The film divides Berlin's day into five acts, building tension through increasingly rapid montage that mirrors the city's accelerating pace.

Ruttmann's technical innovations were groundbreaking. He used hidden cameras to capture candid street scenes, mounted cameras on moving vehicles, and employed split-screen effects. These techniques would later influence documentary pioneers like Jean Vigo in À propos de Nice (1930) and contemporary urban documentarians like Frederick Wiseman in In Jackson Heights (2015). sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue reimagining the city symphony format. Baraka (1992) expanded the scope globally, while London (1994) by Patrick Keiller added philosophical narration to urban observation. Digital technology has enabled new approaches, seen in works like Tokyo! (2008) and Heart of a Dog (2015), but they all trace their DNA back to Ruttmann's pioneering vision of Berlin as a living organism of light and motion.
